intro_title_en: Start with no Chinese: script and chapter preparation
intro_en: Start here with no Chinese assumed. Read the script preparation for your next chapter before its story. If you arrived through a direct chapter link, use How to read to return here first. The preparation is additional to the chapter, its Pensa and its workbook. You can study it in several short sittings.

Read the Chinese horizontally from left to right. A square written form is a character; a word can contain one or more characters. The story has no spaces between its ordinary words. Punctuation separates clauses and speech. Learn the traditional forms shown here; no simplified-script knowledge is assumed.

Roman letters give modern Mandarin citation readings, not reconstructed ancient sounds. A tone mark belongs to the syllable: ā is high and level, á rises, ǎ dips and rises in isolation, à falls. An unmarked syllable is light. Citation tones may change in connected speech. Keep your tongue as for “ee” and round your lips for ü. Xī'ān has two syllables, xī plus ān; xiān is one syllable. You will answer in Chinese characters, without tone-typing or audio tasks.

For typed answers, a traditional-Chinese pinyin input method lets you type the supplied roman reading without tone marks, then choose the exact written character from its candidates. Compare shapes carefully. While learning input, you can copy a form from the visible reference. Pinyin is a lookup aid; its letters do not all have English sound values, and fluent Mandarin pronunciation is not a prerequisite for following these scenes.

A subject is the person or thing a sentence says something about. In the worked examples a person performs an action on a book: the book is the object directly related to that action. Verbs do not take English-style person or tense endings. No word for “a” or “the” is needed in these examples.

Worked contrast: 橋在水中，人在岸。橋有路，人在岸，視水。安在岸，待客。 — A bridge is in the water while a person is on the bank. The bridge has a path; the person looks at the water from the bank. An waits for the guest on the bank.

近 and 遠 can describe a named place without an extra verb meaning “is”: 橋近，山遠。 — The bridge is near; the mountain is far away. Worked contrast: 人有書，書在岸。人視山，止。橋近，安至橋。 — A person has a book, which is on the bank. The person looks at the mountain and stops. The bridge is near and An reaches it. Nearness and distance depend on the people’s current viewpoint, not fixed sizes.

遲 describes lateness: 安遲，寧待安。 — An is late and Ning waits for him. This is not a newly licensed word for walking slowly. Worked continuation: 寧在橋，客在岸。客待安，安至岸。寧視安，立。 — Ning is at a bridge and the guest on a bank. The guest waits for An, who reaches the bank; Ning looks at An and stands.

渡川 — dù chuān — cross the river; the river is the object of 渡. A changed bank after the action makes the result explicit: 安渡川，至東岸。寧在東岸，待安。客在西岸，視川。 — An crosses the river and reaches the east bank, where Ning waits for him. A guest is on the west bank looking at the river. Do not infer an unmentioned crossing merely from a later person’s position.

In 家遠, “the household is far away,” 家 refers to the family household back at home. The spatial context supplies its location; it does not turn 家 into a new general word for a building. Worked scene: 家遠，山近。安在岸，視山。寧在橋，待安。客持紙，安立。 — The household is far away and the mountain near. An looks at the mountain from the bank, Ning waits at the bridge, and the guest holds paper while An stands. Keep the old household distinct from a newly encountered gate.

誰持燈？寧持燈。安持書，客持紙。寧視燈，安視書。門閉，人在門外。 — Who holds the lamp? Ning holds it. 誰 takes the subject position of the unknown person; the answer names that person. The other named holders are separate contrasts, not alternative answers about the same lamp. Try covering the answer and naming the holder in a complete statement.

主，誰也？安不知主。安有書，寧無書。客持紙，紙有姓。安視紙，寧視書。 — The owner—who is it? An does not know the owner. 誰 is the unknown identity in the nominal predicate, followed by the already known 也. 不 denies 知, not the noun 主. Having or holding an object does not identify its owner.

書在何處？書在門外。安持書，寧持燈。人在門內，門閉。客在門外，持紙。 — Where is the book? It is outside the gate. 在 remains the location predicate; 何處 is what place. This is not an interrogative moved before a preposition. Only this where family is practised here; broad how/why and embedded know-who questions wait.

人問。安答。安呼寧，寧應。安視書，寧視紙。客持帙，帙有字。紙有姓。 — A person asks; An answers. 問 and 答 frame separate direct quotations, not a new embedded-question construction. Contrast a call answered by 應. An answer may report uncertainty rather than supply a name.

寧識半字，寧不知主。安視破葉，客視帙字。安持書，寧持燈。客持紙，紙有姓。 — Ning recognises the damaged identifying mark, but does not know the owner. 識 here means recognising that particular half-character or wrapper mark; it does not assert reading arbitrary writing. 知 has the direct object 主, the owner whose identity is unknown.

人指破葉，安視半字。寧持燈，燈明。客持紙，紙有姓。安視帙，帙有字。 — The person points to the damaged leaf; An looks at the half-character. 指 takes the pointed-to object directly. No finger/body noun sense or abstract general reference system is introduced.

誰假燈？寧假燈。人持燈，寧取燈。寧持燈，安持書。客持紙，視姓。 — Who will borrow the lamp? Ning offers to borrow it, and its current holder passes it to her. With a prospective offer and willing handoff, 假 is borrowing/on loan, not lending or being fake. Compare an unexplained taking: custody alone does not establish a loan. The present holder need not be its ultimate owner.

卷全，書不全。卷有全葉，書有破葉。安視全葉，寧視半字。客持紙，紙有姓。 — The fascicle is complete; the book is incomplete. 全 is the already taught whole/complete quality, now predicated and denied with 不. Comparing physical completeness does not prove that two volumes contain the same work or identify an owner.

一半 — yī bàn — one half. 一 is one and 半 is half; here the pair is a substantive, something that can stand as a subject. Practise this expression with the named complementary halves before learning wider quantity patterns. Worked contrast: 安持書，寧持燈。書有破葉，卷有全葉。安視書，寧視卷。 — Track the two distinct objects; incompleteness alone does not show how much is missing.

人指書。人：「書不全。一半在門內，一半在何處？」安視人，寧視書。客持紙，視人。 — The reader points to the book and assesses it: “The book is incomplete. One half is inside the gate; where is the other half?” The paired one-half statements contrast a present part with its unlocated complement. This is his assessment and open question, not narrator arithmetic established merely by a damaged leaf. Try identifying which half is explicitly located and which is being asked about, before checking: first present, second unlocated.

葉在家，家遠。父持二葉，母持小書。先生持紙，紙有「安」字。安視書，寧持燈。 — The leaves are at the household back home; that home is far away. 家 refers to the known family home. Reporting that the leaves are there does not transport them into the present scene or turn 家 into a general new building sense.

人開門。人呼安，安應。安持書入門。寧持燈，客持紙。門內有火，火明。 — The person opens the gate, calls An, and An responds and enters holding the book. This sequence supplies a pragmatic invitation; 呼 itself still means call. Do not silently read a general word for permit into it. Each person’s movement is stated separately.
